html:
A cargo theft investigation begins with speed, safety, and disciplined evidence preservation. Shippers, freight brokers, motor carriers, warehouse operators, insurers, manufacturers, retailers, and attorneys may all need facts after a load disappears, a driver is diverted, or a fraudulent carrier obtains possession. A licensed investigator can develop leads and document events, but does not replace emergency services, law enforcement, the insurer, or legal counsel.

If a theft is active or anyone is in danger, call 911. Do not confront a suspected thief, enter private property, or attempt a recovery without law-enforcement direction. Early decisions should protect people first and preserve information before accounts, devices, messages, or location data change.

Cargo Theft Investigation: What Should Happen First?

Assign one authorized incident lead and record every notification, decision, and incoming fact. Promptly notify the appropriate local law-enforcement agency, the carrier and shipper, the freight broker or logistics provider, the insurer or special investigations unit, and counsel when required. The FBI cargo theft resource advises reporting immediate danger to 911, filing a local or state police report, and contacting the FBI when appropriate.

  1. Confirm the last reliable event. Identify when and where the freight, tractor, trailer, container, seal, and driver were last independently verified.
  2. Freeze routine deletion. Preserve dispatch messages, load-board communications, emails, call logs, GPS or telematics data, gate records, video, and access logs through authorized channels.
  3. Protect original records. Retain source files and exports, note collection times, and avoid editing screenshots or overwriting device data.
  4. Separate facts from assumptions. Record what a system or witness actually shows, the source, and any limitation.
  5. Coordinate outreach. Uncontrolled calls to suspects, drivers, warehouses, or buyers can alert people, create conflicting statements, or interfere with official work.

What Is Cargo Theft?

The FBI defines cargo theft broadly as theft of goods, money, baggage, or other property that forms part of a commercial freight shipment moving in commerce. It can occur from a truck, railcar, vessel, aircraft, warehouse, freight station, distribution facility, yard, or intermodal container.

What Are the Types of Cargo Theft?

Google autocomplete currently surfaces this question. The FBI describes three useful categories:

  • Straight cargo theft: freight is physically stolen from a truck stop, lot, yard, warehouse, rail facility, or other location.
  • Strategic cargo theft: deception causes a shipper, broker, or carrier to release a load to the wrong party. Examples include fictitious pickups, identity theft, account takeover, fraudulent carriers, and double-brokering schemes.
  • Cyber cargo theft: phishing, malware, compromised accounts, or other cyber activity helps criminals obtain shipment data or redirect freight.

The category guides the evidence plan. A cut seal and missing trailer require different leads from a shipment released through a convincing but fraudulent email domain.

What Evidence Should Be Preserved After Cargo Theft?

Useful cargo theft evidence can include the bill of lading, rate confirmation, purchase order, packing list, dispatch history, driver and tractor information, trailer or container number, seal number, pickup and delivery instructions, identity documents received during onboarding, payment details, load-board records, phone numbers, email headers, IP or account alerts, GPS pings, electronic logging data, toll records, gate logs, badge access, surveillance video, photographs, and witness names.

Preserve only information the organization is authorized to access. Do not guess passwords, enter private accounts, track a device without lawful authority, or obtain protected records through deception. When litigation is pending or reasonably anticipated, counsel should guide legal holds, collection scope, privilege, and expert involvement.

A clean chronology is often more useful than a folder of unexplained screenshots. For each item, record its source, collection date, custodian, time zone, and relationship to the shipment. Keep originals and work from copies when possible.

Who Investigates Cargo Theft?

Responsibility may involve local police, state cargo-theft units, federal agencies, insurer SIUs, corporate security teams, cargo-network partners, and licensed private investigators. The FBI states that cases meeting federal thresholds are investigated in collaboration with private-sector and federal, state, and local partners. The National Insurance Crime Bureau also describes coordination among insurers, law enforcement, logistics companies, shippers, and investigative vendors.

A private cargo theft investigator may organize the timeline, verify companies and contact points, canvass relevant public or authorized locations, identify cameras and witnesses, obtain voluntary statements, research lawful public sources, document observable activity, and relay leads through the client's approved reporting channel. Investigators do not execute search warrants, compel records, make prosecutorial decisions, or guarantee recovery.

How Are Carriers and Pickup Identities Verified?

Verification should use contact information obtained independently—not only the phone number or link supplied in a suspicious message. The FMCSA Company Snapshot allows searches by company name, USDOT number, or MC number and provides public identification and safety information. Compare legal names, addresses, authority, known contacts, equipment, insurance information, email domains, and recent changes across reliable sources.

A valid public record does not prove that the person communicating actually represents that carrier. Strategic thieves can impersonate legitimate businesses. Call a previously verified number, confirm pickup and rerouting authority, and examine inconsistencies across documents, timestamps, domains, and devices. For preventive vendor screening, see our due diligence investigation services guide.

How Long Does a Theft Investigation Take?

Google autocomplete shows this as a related question, but there is no universal timeline. Initial triage may take hours because video retention, GPS data, and recovery opportunities can be time-sensitive. A multi-state freight theft investigation involving impersonated carriers, several warehouses, digital evidence, and resale channels may continue for weeks or longer.

Ask for phased milestones: immediate intake and preservation, a verified event timeline, priority witness or location work, interim lead reporting, and a final report. The investigator should identify dependencies and budget limits without promising that the cargo will be found or that a criminal case will result.

How Much Do Cargo Theft Investigation Services Cost?

Fees depend on urgency, hours, jurisdictions, travel, number of locations, surveillance, interviews, database or public-record costs, digital-forensics needs, and reporting requirements. Some agencies bill hourly with a retainer and require approval before additional work. Cyber forensics, specialized tracking, laboratory analysis, or expert testimony may be separate.

Get written terms covering rates, mileage, expenses, after-hours response, authorization thresholds, communication frequency, evidence handling, report format, and stop conditions. A realistic scope prioritizes the leads most likely to expire rather than promising an unlimited nationwide search.

What Should You Ask Before Hiring a Cargo Theft Investigator?

  • Who is licensed in every state where field activity may occur?
  • What experience applies to straight, strategic, fictitious-pickup, double-brokering, or cyber-enabled theft?
  • How will the investigator coordinate with law enforcement, the insurer, counsel, and internal teams?
  • How are source files, time zones, metadata, notes, and chain-of-custody records handled?
  • Which urgent steps are included, and who can authorize more time or travel?
  • Will the report distinguish confirmed facts, witness statements, analytical leads, limitations, and unresolved conflicts?

Miami PI Agency is a licensed Florida private investigative agency. Fieldwork outside Florida is performed by investigators licensed in the state where the activity occurs. The agency does not provide legal advice. Consult qualified counsel about reporting duties, evidence preservation, insurance coverage, employment matters, contract rights, and use of investigative findings.

Request a Confidential Cargo Theft Case Assessment

Prepare the police report number if available, shipment identifiers, last verified location and time, parties and contact points, route, cargo description, estimated value, carrier documents, insurer information, and known deadlines. Do not send sensitive records through an unsecured first-contact message. Request a confidential consultation to discuss lawful scope, jurisdiction, immediate priorities, budget, and reporting.
